report.markdown:
# Speed of Light and the Metre

## Overview

The speed of light in a vacuum is defined as exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, and the metre was redefined in terms of this constant in 1983. [1][2][3][4]

## Sources

1. [Speed of light - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light) — wikipedia.org, published 2001-10-31, fetched 2026-10-31
2. [Meter | NIST](https://www.nist.gov/si-redefinition/meter) — nist.gov, published 2019-05-09, fetched 2026-10-31
3. [How Fast Is the Speed of Light, and How Was It First Measured?](https://physicsfundamentals.org/blog/speed-of-light) — physicsfundamentals.org, published 2026-03-30, fetched 2026-10-31
4. [Metre - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre) — wikipedia.org, published 2001-11-01, fetched 2026-10-31

stats.title: Speed of Light and the Metre

claims.text: The metre was redefined in terms of the speed of light in 1983.

evidence.quote: In 1983 this was updated to a length defined in terms of the speed of light ; this definition was reworded in 2019:
This is not a measured approximation — since 1983, the General Conference on Weights and Measures fixed c at this exact value and redefined the metre accordingly.
Building upon these and other advances, the meter was redefined by international agreement in 1983 as the length of the path traveled by light in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.

claims.text: The speed of light in a vacuum is defined as exactly 299,792,458 m/s.

evidence.quote: The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly c = 299,792,458 m/s .
This definition also locked the speed of light at 299,792,458 meters per second in a vacuum.
As a result of this definition, the value of the speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299 792 458 m/s and has become a defined constant in the SI system of units.
